As my term as President comes to a close I would like to thank all the people on the past and present
Boards of Directors and the many, many volunteers for all the work they have done on behalf of the
Guild. Without all of your help the Guild would not be such a wonderful success. I have enjoyed
working with, and becoming friends with, all of you. When I think back over the last four years (eight
on the Board) the people are what I remember the most. THANKS!
This months General Meeting is also our AGM where we will be presenting the minutes and financial
reports from the last year, and electing a President, a Secretary and three Members At Large. Please
plan to attend so we can count your vote. And if you would like a say in the future of our Guild, please
step up and get nominated for one of the positions. Let me or one of the Board members know if you
are interested or have any questions.
I finally had the time to attend a demonstration and Sally Ault did not disappoint. It was wonderful to
see how she could turn a sea urchin shell into a beautiful box. And I really enjoyed the decorating
techniques she showed. Who would have thought to decorate a turning with egg shells?
I have heard that a few of you may be going to Anacortes March 7th to see Stuart Batty demonstrating. It would be nice if someone could take some photos and let us know how it went in the next
newsletter.
I would like to thank Ed Pretty and all the volunteers who made the Lee Valley ‘Turning Event’ another big success. Bringing awareness to our craft is one of our missions, and this event is a prime
example of how we can be having fun in the community while showing off our talents. I am told that
the display in the entry to the store was a big hit.
Writing these columns, for me, has been one of the hardest things of being President. This is one job I
will not miss.
I wish the new President and Board all the best. We have a strong Guild that can only get better by
building on the foundations the past Boards and volunteers have built.
Happy Turning
Bill

Editor's Notes
This month we will hold our Annual General Meeting (AGM). This is a legal requirement for us to
retain our status as a not-for-profit organization in BC. We are required to present a financial report and to elect Board members and officers consistent with our constitution.
Our table officers – president, vice president, secretary, and treasurer – sever for 2 year terms with
the president and secretary elected in even years and the VP and treasurer elected in odd years. In
addition, board members may serve a maximum of 2 terms (4 years) before having to step down for
at least 1 term.
We have always tried to make these AGMs informative, efficient, and quick. However, we also are
anxious to ensure that any questions or concerns are addressed.
Please attend this month and participate (that means vote) in out AGM. It is a simple way to keep
the Guild running smoothly.
We are always looking for content for the newsletter so please let us know if you have story ideas,
announcements, success stories and so on. Send then to editor@gvwg.ca

We began this session of Tech Talk with a
question concerning a project with a large,
weak bark inclusion that extended to the edge
of the piece. The question was how to salvage
the weak edge. The geometry was such that
using CA glue did not look promising so several suggested masking one side and filling it
with epoxy resin. Robert suggested using duct
tape since the epoxy will not stick to it (nice
trick).
Another suggestion was inserting a butterfly or
row of biscuits and then turning them to the
desired shape
And another suggestion was to NOT try to salvage the edge but to let the inclusion open up
and make that a feature of the piece.
Good discussion all the way around and we
look forward to seeing the finished results.
Next, we talked about holding square pieces of
dressed material so it can be turned on the face
without marking the sides. One member ingeniously used his Coles jaws for this with
great results. Unlike using larger metal jaws
there is much less risk of marking the stock
and a much wider range of stock can be accommodated. Nice trick.
Someone asked about making a tri-point beading tool. These are commercially available as
the one from Ashley Iles shown here:
but they are
easily made
from a used
gouge. Once
the tool has
been ground
to the bottom
of the flute
there is still
excellent tempered steel
left. Grinding
a three-sided pyramid on the end yields a great
general-purpose beading tool. I will speak to
Phil about doing an FoF session on how to use
this versatile tool.
Barry finished the session by showing some
plastic finish storage bags he found on eBay.
For those not familiar with them you might
check out the Lee Valley offering at:
http://www.leevalley.com/en/wood/
page.aspx?p=72867&cat=1,190,44133
I have been storing Tung Oil and Wipe-on Poly
in these bags for 2 years now and have had no
loss due to evaporation or oxidation. I highly
recommend them for storing any of our finishing products.
We always hold a Tech Talk session starting at
6:30 on meeting nights. Please bring your
questions, solutions and ideas to the next session on Feb 22nd.
By Bruce Campbell

Focus On Fundamentals
Dan Breck ‐ On Rolling Pins
Page 5
GVWG
Dan started by stating that most of the focus we
have with the various demonstrators is on techniques, artistically pleasing forms, tools and safety.
What we don’t get is instruction on functional
forms. Often we make things we want to use but we
don’t consider the end user.
Dan’s wife wanted a French rolling pin and he didn’t have a clue what a French rolling pin was, so he
went on the Internet to find the details of a rolling
pin, size, shape and how to use it. He found next to
no information but did find a website by a pastry
chef. The chef formed a panel of pastry chef’s and
had them test the leading brands of rolling pins
and then asked them what they liked or not liked
about them
The study looked at the sizes of the standard, marble rolling pins and what they were good for. The
study found that the French rolling pin was the
best for pastry. The standard size of a French rolling pin is around 20” long though that varies
somewhat. The shape varies. For a pastry chef you
want a 10” flat section in the middle for rolling out
pastry then a gradual taper 5” to each end. The diameter of the pin can vary to the size of the user.
In the photo below one pin is 1.75” diameter and
the other 2”. There is a big functional difference in
that range but those are the diameters you want to
work within.
Dan starts with a 2”X2” blank, turns it round and
then turns it down to his target diameter. You can
use a skew or spindle roughing gouge for this but
strive for a smooth surface to reduce sanding. Then
use a sanding block with a hard backing for sanding to retain the smooth surface.
The hardest part of turning rolling pins is getting
the two ends the same. A little extra care at this
point will yield a much nicer product.
Commercial rolling pins are often squared off but
can be very uncomfortable to use. Round off the
ends making yours much “nicer”.
Sanding is done under power until 320 grit. Then
Dan stops the lathe and sands with the grain at 320

Page 6
GVWG
and 400 grit. This helps to eliminate the crossgrain scratches that often occur when spindle
sanding.
Dan finishes with a single a coat of Watco oil, allows it to dry and then sands it with the grain using
400 grit abrasive to knock off the raised grain.
The study form the website tried various woods
including European Beech, Hard Maple and Black
Walnut. The Walnut was the best because they
found that it held the right amount of flour so it
didn’t stick to the dough.
Dan concluded his talk by saying that a rolling pin
is easy to turn and if you make it right you have a
tool that a pastry chef will love

You first need to obtain a nice sea urchin. The
Sputnik versions are sold by Craft Supply USA and
others. The Alfonso, Purple, Green and White Mexican Urchins are a bit harder to find but Etsy and
EBay are good sources. You might even have a local source…or a beach to find them on.
To make the sea Urchin strong you fill it with insulating foam. I use a brand from Home Depot called
Great Stuff. I prefer the type for windows because
doesn’t expand quite as much.
First completely cover the sea urchin with plastic
wrap or foil and masking tape to prevent any of the
foam from getting on the shell. Cut a large hole in
the tape and plastic covering the hole at the top.
Squirt in the foam being sure to get it into all the
areas. It will continue to “grow” until it gets firm so
don’t overfill. I goes everywhere and you will soon
see why it is important to cover the shell completely with plastic wrap. If you overfill with too small a
hole it can break the shell. If you get foam on the
shell it will discolor in time even if you think you
got it cleaned off. Once the foam is cured remove
the tape and plastic wrap.
Note that you won’t use the whole can of foam unless you are doing a large number of urchins but if
you don’t clean the tube with acetone immediately
you won’t be able to use it again.
To determine the size of wood blank required you
need to decide what the diameter of the rim of the
box insert will be and add a bit for rounding to a
cylinder. Measure the height of the urchin to determine the length of wood needed for the insert,
add the desired height of the lid and the foot
(including a longer than usual tenon) plus the
amount of wood needed for 2 tenons and 2 parting
cuts and that is the length of blank you will need
for the box. If you want a finial from the same
wood add that length to the blank or find a pen
blank that is the same wood to use for the finial. A
contrasting finial or one made from a different material can be effective too.
Round the blank to a cylinder, make a tenon on
both ends and part between the base and the lid.
Put the base into the chuck and form the lip that
will overlap the hole in the shell. Shape the outside
of the box (this part won’t be seen) to the desired
depth. Create a small tenon on the bottom for insurance.
Cut in a step for the lid to rest on making sure it
being cut into solid wood. If you make the interior
too wide you may cut off the rim of the box. Make
sure the sides of the recess for the lid are perfectly
straight and deep enough to provide a stable spot
for the lid.
Hollow the inside remembering that it shouldn’t be
too deep since it is a small box. I generally make
the depth about the same dimension as the width
of the interior. I gently round the bottom rather
than making straight sides.
(Continued on page 8)
by Sally Ault
Making a Sea Urchin Box

Page 8
GVWG
Sand and finish the rim and inside. No need to finish the outside since it will be hidden inside the
shell.
Put the lid blank into the chuck. Determine the
width of the lid and the width of the tenon which
will fit into the recess in the base of the box. Give
some thought to how the rim of the base and lid
shapes work together. The lid can be wider than
the rim of the base, the same diameter or narrower. It is a design choice. Make sure the tenon on the
lid is perfectly straight. The fit should not be tight -
this is a one handed opening box and you don’t
need a tight fit to work on the lid.
Once the tenon is the right size, create a slight
dovetail inside the tenon going deep enough to get
into solid wood and then create a curved recess in
the lid. Sand and Finish the tenon, rim and inside
the lid.
Rough out the shape of the top of the lid as far as
possible while it is still in the chuck. You can support the lid using the tailstock with a non-marring
insert while you are shaping. Once you are close to
the desired shape part it off (the wood remaining
in the chuck is for the foot) and turn it around in a
chuck with the jaws expanding into the lids dovetail recess. I use a piece of paper towel to help
avoid any marks from the chuck jaws. Support the
lid with the tailstock. (I use an extension point with
the smallest pin) and finish turning the top of the
lid. Take very light cuts.
If you are making a tall finial you can make the finial separately from the lid with a 1/8” or ¼” tenon
on the end…make the corresponding recess in the
lid and connect them after both the lid and finial
are completed.
For the foot, measure the area to be covered by the
shell side of the foot. Round to a cylinder and cut a
tenon that will be inserted into the shell. Cut a
small tenon on the end of that tenon to use when
finishing the bottom of the foot.
Shape the part of the foot that will touch the shell
with an undercut so the shell will fit up into it if
needed.
Shape the outside of the foot making sure the base
is wide enough to give support to the shell. Part off
(Continued from page 7)

Page 9
GVWG
as much of an undercut as possible so there isn’t as
much turning to do when it is turned around in the
chuck. Sand and finish all the accessible areas.
Secure the small tenon into the chuck and support
the foot area with the tailstock for as long as possible. Again I use the extension point with the smallest pin for this. Shape the underside of the foot as
far as possible then remove the tailstock and complete the cutting. Sand and finish the underside. If
you make a foot with a pedestal it can be made in
one piece or in two pieces similar to adding a finial.
Using a rotary tool with a small cylindrical sander
or abrasive bit, start cutting out the shell to the diameter of the insert. Measure carefully and draw a
line at the proper diameter. Shape the hole slowly
so you don’t crack off any shell. Keep trying the
insert. Only take as much foam out as needed.
Don’t make the shell too tight against the wood in
case of movement of the wood. Glue insert into the
shell with 5 minute epoxy.
Using a smaller abrasive bit make the hole for the
foot tenon in the bottom. Keep trying for size…
again don’t make the fit too tight.
If you have a tall finial and/or a pedestal foot you
will need to take extra care to line them up since
shells are not symmetrical. Glue in the foot with 5
minute epoxy.
Sally Ault visited us last month and entertained us with an all-day demonstration on
Saturday and six lucky members spent an
all-day hands-on class with her on Sunday.
Sally was kind enough to leave us with this
step-by-step for making her Sea Urchin
boxes.
Thanks very much, Sally.
